lesson.title: Rounding Up the Reds: The Palmer Raids
lesson.summary: Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer directed a series of mass arrests of suspected radicals in late 1919 and early 1920, a campaign marked by warrantless raids, denial of due process, and the deportation of hundreds of immigrants.
lesson.body:
Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, whose own home had been bombed in June 1919, emerged as the government's chief crusader against the Red Scare, and some historians have noted his ambitions for the 1920 Democratic presidential nomination likely sharpened his zeal. He put a young Justice Department official named J. Edgar Hoover in charge of a new General Intelligence Division, which compiled files on tens of thousands of suspected radicals, socialists, anarchists, and labor organizers across the country. Using this intelligence, Palmer organized a series of raids on homes, meeting halls, and union offices, first in November 1919 and then in a much larger sweep on the night of January 2, 1920, which hit more than thirty cities simultaneously.

The raids trampled basic civil liberties. Justice Department agents entered homes and offices without search warrants, arrested people without formal charges, and held many suspects for days without access to a lawyer. Several thousand people were detained in the January raids alone, most of them immigrants targeted simply for their political associations or their membership in immigrant fraternal and labor organizations, not because they had committed any specific crime. Because immigration law allowed the deportation of noncitizen radicals, many detainees faced not criminal trial but expulsion from the country. The most famous case was the deportation of the anarchists Emma Goldman and Alexander Berkman, who were placed aboard the army transport ship Buford in December 1919, along with roughly two hundred and fifty other deportees, and sent to Soviet Russia. Newspapers nicknamed the vessel the Soviet Ark.

The backlash came quickly once the initial panic faded. Louis F. Post, the Assistant Secretary of Labor responsible for reviewing deportation orders, canceled hundreds of them for lack of evidence, drawing furious attacks from Palmer's allies in Congress, though Post was later vindicated. In May 1920, a group of prominent lawyers, including future Supreme Court justice Felix Frankfurter and legal scholar Zechariah Chafee, published a widely read report documenting the raids' illegal searches, coerced statements, and abuse of detainees. Palmer further discredited himself by publicly predicting a massive radical uprising on May Day 1920 that simply never happened. The episode helped spur the founding of the American Civil Liberties Union in early 1920, an organization created specifically to defend the constitutional rights the Red Scare had trampled, and it stands today as one of the starkest examples in American history of civil liberties abandoned in the name of national security.
